title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
Definition: a system made of several quantum subsystems described jointly via the tensor product.
Hilbert space

1 qubit → \(\mathbb{C}^2\)
2 qubits → \(\mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2\), dimension \(4\)
\(n\) qubits → \((\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n} = \mathbb{C}^{2^n}\), dimension \(2^n\)

Canonical 2-qubit basis: \(\{|00\rangle, |01\rangle, |10\rangle, |11\rangle\}\)
General state: \(|\Psi\rangle = \alpha_{00}|00\rangle + \alpha_{01}|01\rangle + \alpha_{10}|10\rangle + \alpha_{11}|11\rangle\), with \(\sum|\alpha_{ij}|^2 = 1\).
Tensor product
\[A \otimes B = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11}B & \cdots & a_{1m}B \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_{n1}B & \cdots & a_{nm}B \end{bmatrix}\]

Third type of multiplication (after scalar and matrix multiplication)
Associative: \(A \otimes (B \otimes C) = (A \otimes B) \otimes C\)
Resulting matrix: \(nn' \times mm'\)

Product state: \(|\Psi\rangle = |\psi_1\rangle \otimes |\psi_2\rangle\) → independent subsystems, describable separately.
Entangled state: cannot be written as a tensor product of individual states → phenomenon with no classical analogue.
Classical simulation limit: for \(N \approx 300\) qubits, \(2^N \gg 10^{82}\) > number of atoms in the universe → classical simulation is impossible.

title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
Definition: an entangled state is a state of a composite system that cannot be written as \(|\psi_1\rangle \otimes |\psi_2\rangle\) for any choice of individual states.
Bell pair (emblematic state)
\[|\Phi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)\]
Proof of entanglement: if it were a tensor product, then \(\alpha\beta' = 0\) AND \(\beta\alpha' = 0\) AND \(\alpha\alpha' = \beta\beta' = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \neq 0\) → contradiction.
Product vs. entangled test: rank-1 condition → \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11} = \alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}\)
Non-classical properties

Non-separability: the state of each particle cannot be described separately, regardless of distance
Non-local correlations: the state contains only information about correlations, not about individual particles
Correlated collapse: measuring one particle → instantaneous and coherent collapse of the other
No superluminal information transmission (each individual outcome remains random)

Generation via a circuit: \(|00\rangle \xrightarrow{H \otimes I} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |10\rangle) \xrightarrow{\text{CNOT}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)\)
Role: fundamental resource of quantum computing along with superposition and interference. Used in: teleportation, QKD, Shor/Grover algorithms, error correction.

title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
Definition: process by which a quantum system loses its superposition and entanglement through interaction with the external environment.
Mechanism: the environment performs “involuntary measurements” on the system → superpositions fade → classical behavior.
Analogy: a coin balanced on its edge (superposition) → the slightest contact makes it fall (collapse).
Consequences for quantum computing

Destruction of superposition → loss of quantum interference
Erosion of entanglement → reduced algorithmic advantage
Limitation of circuit depth (the computation must finish before the coherence time)
Main source of quantum errors in current devices

NISQ link: decoherence → Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum devices (~100 controllable qubits, but noise prevents complex algorithms like Shor).
Technical countermeasures

Extreme isolation from the environment (superconducting qubits: a few millikelvins)
Long decoherence times
Fast quantum gates (duration ≪ coherence time)

Theoretical solution: quantum error correction (QEC) → 1 logical qubit encoded into \(N\) physical qubits. Principle: correct errors faster than they occur. Recently: a Google experiment (101 physical qubits) showing a reduction of the effective error rate.

title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
Measurement = irreversible, probabilistic, destructive act (≠ classical readout, which is non-perturbative).
Born rule: for \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\): \[\Pr[|0\rangle] = |\alpha|^2, \quad \Pr[|1\rangle] = |\beta|^2\] → classical outcome + irreversible collapse (all information about the other amplitude is lost).
Compare two experiments: Hadamard gate









Experiment A (with intermediate measurement)
Experiment B (no intermediate measurement)




Circuit
\(|0\rangle \to H \to \text{measure} \to H \to \text{measure}\)
\(|0\rangle \to H \to H \to \text{measure}\)


Result
\(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\) with prob. \(\frac{1}{2}\) (random)
\(|0\rangle\) with prob. \(1\) (deterministic)



Explanation by quantum interference

Without measurement: path amplitudes add or cancel (constructive/destructive interference). In B: \(H^2 = I\), paths to \(|1\rangle\) cancel.
With measurement: the superposition is destroyed → no interference → random outcome.

Fundamental algorithmic implication: measurements must be placed only at the end of the circuit, after constructive amplification of the correct answers and cancellation of the wrong ones.
Distinguishing orthogonal states: \(|+\rangle\) vs. \(|-\rangle\) are indistinguishable in the standard basis, but after \(H\): \(H|+\rangle = |0\rangle\) and \(H|-\rangle = |1\rangle\) → perfect discrimination by choosing the right measurement basis.

Shor’s algorithm: reduces factorization to finding the period of \(f(s) = x^s \bmod N\) via the QFT. Direct threat to RSA (requires ~8000 logical qubits for RSA-2048).
Grover’s algorithm: quadratic speedup, provably optimal for unstructured search. Universal but modest.
Quantum simulation: most promising application (Feynman, 1981) → quantum chemistry, drug discovery, materials, high-energy physics.
NISQ (hybrid) algorithms

VQE: computes the ground-state energy of a Hamiltonian (classical–quantum loop)
QAOA: combinatorial optimization with a parameterized circuit

Fundamental limit: quantum computers do not solve general NP-hard problems. Advantage only for problems with exploitable mathematical structure (periodicity, uniform amplitude, Hamiltonian structure).

title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
Motivation: the raw number of qubits does not reflect real power → need a metric capturing quality and quantity.
Definition (Moll et al., Quantum Science and Technology, 3, 030503, 2018)
\[\tilde{V}_Q = \min[N, d(N)]^2\]
where \(N\) = number of qubits, \(d(N)\) = circuit depth that can be executed reliably on \(N\) qubits.
IBM version: \[\log_2 V_Q = \arg\max_{n \leq N}\{\min[n, d(n)]\}\]
Interpretation: size of the largest square circuit (qubits × depth) executable reliably. Limited by the weaker factor between width and depth.
What limits \(d(N)\): decoherence, gate errors, limited connectivity, measurement fidelity.

title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
Context: given a qubit that is either \(|\psi_a\rangle\) or \(|\psi_b\rangle\) with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) each, what is the maximum probability of discriminating them by measurement?
Special case: if \(\langle\psi_a|\psi_b\rangle = 0\) (orthogonal) → perfect discrimination (\(p = 1\)) via \(U^\dagger\) mapping to the computational basis.
Helstrom–Holevo bound
\[p_\text{success} \leq \frac{1}{2}(1 + \sin\theta)\]
where \(\cos\theta = |\langle\psi_a|\psi_b\rangle|\), \(\theta \in [0, \pi/2]\).
The bound is achieved (exact optimum, not only an upper bound).

Optimal measurement: eigenbasis of \(|\psi_a\rangle\langle\psi_a| - |\psi_b\rangle\langle\psi_b|\).

Answer: No. The no-signalling principle forbids it.

title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
Statement: there is no unitary transformation \(U\) such that: \[U(|\psi\rangle|0\rangle) = |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle \quad \forall |\psi\rangle\]
Proof by contradiction (linearity + isometry of \(U\))
Assume a universal \(U\). Then for any two states \(|\psi\rangle, |\phi\rangle\):
\[\underbrace{\langle\psi|\phi\rangle}_{\text{left side}} = \underbrace{(\langle\psi|\phi\rangle)^2}_{\text{right side}}\]
→ \(x = x^2\) → only \(x = 0\) or \(x = 1\) → states are orthogonal or identical.
→ Any pair of distinct non-orthogonal states cannot be cloned. Contradiction.
Why cloning would violate physics

Would violate the no-signalling principle (tomography via copies + entanglement → superluminal info)
Would enable super-compression forbidden by Holevo’s theorem (1 qubit = 1 bit of classical information)

Practical consequences

Error correction: no naive redundancy by copying → entangled codes required
QKD (BB84): an eavesdropper cannot copy qubits without leaving a trace → security guaranteed
Only orthogonal states are “copyable” → classical information only

title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
Statement: there is no unitary transformation \(\tilde{U}\) such that: \[\tilde{U}(|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle) = |\psi\rangle|0\rangle \quad \forall |\psi\rangle\]
Relation to no-cloning: time-reversal dual (the forbidden \(2 \to 1\) copies transition mirrors the forbidden \(1 \to 2\) transition).
Proof by reversibility: if \(\tilde{U}\) existed → its adjoint \(\tilde{U}^\dagger\) would implement \(|\psi\rangle|0\rangle \to |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle\) → cloning → contradiction with no-cloning.
Physical meaning: quantum information is conserved under unitary evolution — it can neither be created ex nihilo (no-cloning) nor annihilated (no-deleting).

⚠️ Nuance: measurement (non-unitary) can “destroy” a superposition, but this is not deleting in the sense of the theorem (it is irreversible and non-unitary).

Practical implications for quantum circuits

Ancilla qubits introduced during computation cannot simply be erased
They must be returned to their initial state by inverse operations (\(U^\dagger\))
This complicates algorithm design

Consistency of the three principles:

No-cloning → forbids increasing quantum information
No-deleting → forbids decreasing it
Measurement → the only operation that “destroys” a superposition, at the cost of fundamental irreversibility

title: Question 1 — Qubit definition
text:
Summary
5 major families of applications
1. Factorization (Shor’s algorithm, 1994)

Classical complexity: sub-exponential \(O(e^{n^{1/3}})\)
Quantum complexity: polynomial \(O(n^3 \log n)\)
Key mechanism: QFT to find the period of \(f(s) = x^s \bmod N\)
Impact: direct threat to RSA (~8000 logical qubits for RSA-2048)

2. Search (Grover’s algorithm, 1997)

\(O(N) \to O(\sqrt{N})\) queries (quadratic speedup, provably optimal)
Applications: unstructured databases, function inversion
Forces doubling key sizes in symmetric cryptography

3. Quantum simulation (Feynman, ~1981)

Simulating \(N\) particles: \(2^N\) classical equations vs \(N\) qubits
Applications: quantum chemistry, drug discovery, materials, lattice QCD
VQE (hybrid): minimizes \(\langle\psi(\theta)|H|\psi(\theta)\rangle\) by adjusting \(\theta\) via a classical optimizer

4. Quantum optimization

Parallel exploration via superposition (e.g., binary quadratic forms minimization)
Domains: logistics, finance, VLSI, operations research
⚠️ Quantum advantage not yet proven for these problems

5. Quantum networks

Key distribution (QKD), certified randomness, distributed computing
Building blocks: quantum teleportation + superdense coding

Post-quantum urgency: cryptographic migration before ~2030–2035. Solutions: lattice-based cryptography, strengthened hashing, QKD. Standardization in progress at NIST.
Technical challenges: decoherence, error correction (\(N\) physical qubits per logical qubit), scaling.

title: Quantum error correction — Quiz
text:
### Why do quantum computers require error correction while modern classical computers do not?

> Think about the physical nature of qubits and their interaction with their environment.

1. [ ] Quantum processors calculate too fast to detect errors
1. [ ] Classical and quantum errors are the same but more frequent
1. [x] Qubits are physically fragile and inevitably interact with their environment, causing errors
    > Correct: qubits (trapped atoms, photons, superconducting circuits) are sensitive to external disturbances, which makes errors inevitable without correction.
1. [ ] Error correction is only necessary for cryptography algorithms


### In Binary Symmetric Channel, what happens if the error rate is p_e = 0.5?

> Think about what a 50% inversion probability for each bit means.

1. [ ] The channel transmits information with a correctable error rate
1. [ ] We can invert the bits received to recover the information
1. [ ] The channel is optimal and no correction is necessary
1. [x] No information can be retrieved from the channel
    > Correct: If p_e = 0.5, each bit is as likely to be correct as incorrect. The channel does not carry any useful information.


### What are the three fundamental obstacles that prevent classical error correction from being directly applied to qubits?

> There are exactly three structural reasons related to the properties of quantum mechanics.

- [x] The no-cloning principle prohibits copying an unknown quantum state
    > Correct: The No-Cloning Theorem is a direct obstacle to the classical repetition strategy.
- [ ] Qubits are too expensive to make in large numbers
    > Incorrect: Hardware cost is not a theoretical barrier to error correction.
- [x] Measurement destroys quantum information by collapse of superposition
    > Correct: any measurement of a superimposed state causes it to collapse, which would destroy the information to be protected.
- [x] Quantum errors are continuous, not discrete as in classical
    > Correct: an alpha|0> + beta|1> qubit can undergo a continuous disturbance on complex coefficients.
- [ ] Quantum gates cannot be combined with measurements
    > Incorrect: Gates and measurements can coexist in a quantum circuit.


### What is the residual error probability after encoding by the classic 3-bit repetition code?

> Remember how many bits need to be flipped for the majority vote to fail.

1. [ ] p_e' = p_e^2
1. [ ] p_e' = 2p_e(1 - p_e)
1. [x] p_e' = 3p_e^2(1 - p_e) + p_e^3
    > Correct: An error occurs if exactly 2 bits (3 ways) or all 3 bits are inverted simultaneously.
1. [ ] p_e' = p_e / 3


### In the 3-qubit bit-flip code (Three-Qubit Bit-Flip Code), how is the logic state alpha|0> + beta|1> encoded?

> It's not a copy of the three qubits — think of what the CNOT gates produce from |00>.

1. [ ] (alpha|0> + beta|1>) tensor (alpha|0> + beta|1>) tensor (alpha|0> + beta|1>)
1. [x] alpha|000> + beta|111>
    > Correct: The encoding produces an entangled state of the three qubits. It's not three independent copies of the logical state.
1. [ ] alpha|010> + beta|101>
1. [ ] (alpha + beta)(|000> + |111>)


### What does a phase-flip error act on a qubit in the computational basis?

> Think about the action of gate Z on |0> and |1>.

1. [ ] It sends |0> on |1> and |1> on |0>
1. [x] It leaves |0> unchanged and sends |1> to -|1>
    > Correct: Gate Z applies |0> -> |0> and |1> -> -|1>. In the computational base, |0> is unchanged.
1. [ ] It sends |+> to |+> and |-> to |->
1. [ ] It applies a rotation of 90 degrees in the XY plane of the Bloch sphere

title: Quantum error correction — Quiz
text:
Level 2 — Comprehension

### Why don't parity-check measurements in bit-flipping code destroy the quantum state?

> Think about what information these measurements reveal — and what information they don't provide access to.

1. [ ] Because they are performed on ancilla qubits, not directly on logical qubits
1. [ ] Because they use Hadamard gates which preserve coherence
1. [x] Because they only reveal the presence of an error, without ever revealing the values ​​of alpha and beta
    > Correct: the M1 and M2 measurements compare the qubits two by two (parity) without accessing the superposition coefficients. The logical state remains intact.
1. [ ] Because they are carried out after the correction, not before


### Why is a phase error (Z) equivalent to a bit flip (X) in the Hadamard basis {|+>, |->}?

> Remember how gate Z transforms |+> and |->.

1. [ ] Because gates X and Z commute in this base
1. [ ] Because |+> and |-> are eigenstates of gate Z
1. [x] Because gate Z exchanges |+> and |->, exactly like gate X exchanges |0> and |1>
    > Correct: Z|+> = |-> and Z|-> = |+>. A phase reversal in the computational base is therefore a bit reversal in the Hadamard basis.
1. [ ] Because the Hadamard and computational bases are orthogonal


### Shor's code is constructed by concatenation of two codes. In what order are they applied and what type of error does each level protect?

> Think about the two levels of Shor's code structure: the inner blocks and the outer level.

1. [x] External level: phase reversal code (3 blocks); internal level: bit flip code (in each block of 3 qubits)
    > Correct: the phase code protects the 3 blocks between them (Z errors), the bit-flip code protects each block of 3 qubits individually (X errors).
1. [ ] External level: bit flip code; internal level: phase reversal code
1. [ ] Both levels protect against the same types of errors to increase robustness
1. [ ] Shor's code does not use concatenation but a single layer of protection


### What is “Digitization of Errors” in the context of quantum error correction?

> This is the phenomenon that resolves the third obstacle identified (continuous errors).

1. [ ] Converting qubits into classical bits to correct them
1. [ ] The use of digital gates instead of analog gates
1. [x] The fact that parity measurements collapse a continuous error to one of four discrete cases: no error, bit-flip, phase-flip, or both
    > Correct: even if the error is continuously parameterized by a, b, c, d, the measurement projects the state onto one of the four discrete subspaces. We only correct 4 types of errors.
1. [ ] The conversion of analog noise into digital signal using quantum hardware


### In the Depolarizing Channel, a qubit undergoes a bit-flip with probability p_e/3. What is the total probability of error?

> The depolarizing channel distributes the noise equally between three types of errors.

1. [ ] p_e / 9
1. [ ] p_e / 3
1. [ ] 2p_e / 3
1. [x] p_e
    > Correct: p_e/3 (bit-flip) + p_e/3 (phase-flip) + p_e/3 (bit+phase-flip) = p_e. The probability of remaining unchanged is 1 - p_e.


### What is the fundamental difference between the encoded state alpha|000> + beta|111> and three independent copies of alpha|0> + beta|1>?

> Remember the no-cloning theorem and the nature of entanglement.

- [x] The alpha|000> + beta|111> state is an entangled state of the three qubits, not a tensor product of three identical qubits
    > Correct: if the three qubits were in independent copies, the state would be (alpha|0>+beta|1>) tensor (alpha|0>+beta|1>) tensor (alpha|0>+beta|1>), which is different and would require knowing alpha and beta.
- [x] Producing three independent copies would violate the no-cloning theorem
    > Correct: This is precisely why we use entanglement. We cannot copy an unknown quantum state.
- [ ] The two states are physically identical but noted differently
- [ ] The tangled state is easier to produce than three independent copies


### The Hamming code (7.4) encodes 4 bits into 7 bits. How does it detect and locate an error?

> Think about the role of the parity check matrix H and the syndrome p = Hc mod 2.

1. [ ] By comparing the received word with all valid code words stored in memory
1. [ ] By repeating the transmission three times and voting
1. [x] By calculating the syndrome p = Hc mod 2: if p = 000 no error, otherwise the 7 possible non-zero values ​​indicate the position of the unique error
    > Correct: The 7 non-zero 3-bit strings correspond to the 7 possible positions of a single error. This is the advantage of linear codes.
1. [ ] By measuring the Hamming distance between the received word and the sent word

title: Quantum error correction — Quiz
text:
Level 3 — Mastery

### A logical qubit is encoded with the bit-flip code on 3 qubits. After passing through a noisy channel, the parity measurements give M1 = 1 and M2 = 1. Which qubit underwent a bit-flip and what correction should be applied?

> Consult the detection table: M1 compares qubits 1 and 2, M2 compares qubits 2 and 3.

1. [ ] Qubit 1 — correction X tensor I tensor I
1. [x] Qubit 2 — correction I tensor
    > Correct: M1=1 indicates that qubits 1 and 2 differ, M2=1 indicates that qubits 2 and 3 differ. Qubit 2 is therefore in disagreement with the other two -> it is he who was reversed.
1. [ ] Qubit 3 — correction I tensor I tensor
1. [ ] No qubits — measurements indicate no errors


### A general error on the first qubit of the Shor code is described by |0> -> a|0> + b|1> and |1> -> c|0> + d|1>. After the parity measurements, why can we correct this state despite the continuity of a, b, c, d?

> Remember the phenomenon of digitalization and the effect of measurements on the superposition of error types.

1. [ ] Because the coefficients a, b, c, d must necessarily be close to 0 or 1 for a real physical channel
1. [ ] Because Shor's code has enough qubits to correct all continuous errors simultaneously
1. [x] Because parity measurements collapse the state onto one of four discrete cases (I, X, Z, XZ), transforming a continuous error into a correctable discrete error
    > Correct: the superposition k·(no error) + l·(bit-flip) + m·(phase-flip) + n·(bit+phase-flip) collapses on a single case during measurement. Correcting this discrete case is enough.
1. [ ] Because continuous errors do not exist in practice — only discrete reversals occur


### Comparison of Shor and Steane codes: which of these statements is correct?

> Think about the parameters of each code: number of physical qubits, encoded logical qubits, and correctness guarantees.

- [x] Steane's code encodes 1 logical qubit into 7 physical qubits, compared to 9 for Shor's code
    > Correct: Steane's code is more efficient with a rate of 1/7 compared to 1/9 for Shor's code.
- [x] Both codes correct any bit-flip and/or phase-flip error on a single qubit
    > Correct: the two codes offer the same guarantees of correction, but with different effectiveness.
- [ ] Shor's code can correct errors on 2 qubits simultaneously, unlike Steane's code
    > Incorrect: neither guarantees error correction on two qubits simultaneously in its basic version.
- [x] Steane's code is a CSS code built from Hamming's code (7.4)
    > Correct: Steane's code is the canonical example of CSS (Calderbank-Shor-Steane) code derived from classic linear code.
- [ ] Shor's code removes the error at O(p_e^3) while Steane's code only removes it at O(p_e^2)
    > Incorrect: both codes remove the error from the depolarizing channel from p_e to O(p_e^2).


### Put the steps for correcting a general error with Shor's code in the correct order.

> Think about the sequential diagram: first the bit-flip errors, then the phase-flip errors.

1. Encoding of the logical state on 9 qubits (concatenation of the two codes)
2. Passage into the noisy channel (any error affects at most one qubit)
3. Parity measurement on each block of 3 qubits to detect a bit-flip
4. Possible correction of the bit-flip identified by the measurements
5. Parity measurement between the three blocks to detect a phase-flip
6. Possible correction of the identified phase-flip
7. Recovery of the original logical state


### Under what hypothesis can we model a general noisy channel as a depolarizing channel after application of error correction?

> Think about the condition on the errors of the different physical qubits composing the code.

1. [ ] Errors must be only bit-flip type, not phase-flip type
1. [x] Errors on different physical qubits must be independent of each other
    > Correct: the independence of errors between qubits makes it possible to decompose the analysis and treat each qubit as independently subjected to a depolarizing channel.
1. [ ] The error rate p_e must be less than 0.1
1. [ ] The physical channel must be a depolarizing channel exactly, without approximation


### Put in the correct order the steps for constructing Shor's code from the two basic codes.

> Shor's code first concatenates the phase code, then applies the bit-flip code to each resulting block.

1. Starting from the logical state alpha|0> + beta|1>
2. Apply the phase reversal code: obtain alpha|+++> + beta|--->
3. Apply CNOT gates to create three tangled blocks of 3 qubits each
4. Apply Hadamard gates on each qubit to obtain the blocks (|000>+|111>) and (|000>-|111>)
5. Obtain the logical state encoded on 9 qubits: |0_L> or |1_L>


### Is the classical 3-bit repetition code directly transposable to the problem of quantum error correction?

1. [ ] TRUE
1. [x] False
    > False: three fundamental obstacles stand in the way — the principle of non-cloning (impossible to copy a quantum state), destructive measurement (which erases superposition), and the continuity of quantum errors. We must adapt the strategy with entanglement and parity measures.


### What is the code rate of Steane's code, and how is it advantageous over Shor's code?

> The code rate is the ratio between the number of logical qubits encoded and the number of physical qubits used.

1. [ ] 1/9 — identical to Shor's code, so no advantage
1. [ ] 1/3 — identical to 3-qubit codes, but with stronger guarantees
1. [x] 1/7 — greater than 1/9 of Shor's code, therefore more efficient for the same correction guarantees
    > Correct: Steane's code uses 7 physical qubits for 1 logical qubit (rate 1/7), compared to 9 for Shor's code (rate 1/9). Both correct the same types of errors.
1. [ ] 4/7 — identical to the Hamming code (7.4) from which it is derived
    > Incorrect: Steane's code encodes 1 quantum logical qubit (not 4 classical bits) into 7 physical qubits. The quantum rate is 1/7.


### In the context of the depolarizing channel, what does "removing the error a O(p_e^2)" mean for a quantum corrector code?

> Compared with the analysis of classical repeating code and its residual error probability.

1. [ ] The code can correct two independent errors simultaneously with certainty
1. [ ] The error is reduced by half compared to p_e
1. [x] For a low error rate p_e, the residual error probability after correction is proportional to p_e^2, which is much smaller than p_e
    > Correct: if p_e = 0.01, then p_e^2 = 0.0001 — a reduction by a factor of 100. Correction requires at least 2 qubits to be simultaneously in error to fail.
1. [ ] Code requires twice as many qubits to cut error in half


### What property of parity measurements makes it possible to simultaneously resolve obstacles 2 and 3 identified for quantum error correction?

> Obstacle 2 concerns the destruction of quantum information. Obstacle 3 concerns the continuity of errors.

1. [ ] Parity measurements are fast, so they don't have time to destroy consistency
1. [x] They only reveal the presence or absence of error (not the values ​​of alpha and beta), and their result collapses the state onto a discrete case, thus digitalizing the continuous errors
    > Correct: on the one hand, parity measurements preserve the logical state by giving no information about alpha and beta. On the other hand, their result (0 or 1) automatically discretizes the continuous error.
1. [ ] They use ancilla qubits which absorb noise without affecting logic qubits
1. [ ] They are reversible, so the quantum information can be restored after the measurement

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 1 — Qubit

### What condition must the state of a qubit $|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle$ satisfy?

> Think about the fact that measurement probabilities must sum to 1.

1. [ ] $\alpha + \beta = 1$
1. [ ] $|\alpha| + |\beta| = 1$
1. [x] $|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1$
    > Correct: this is the normalization condition. Squared complex amplitudes give probabilities, which must sum to 1.
1. [ ] $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = 0$


### According to the Born rule, what is the probability of observing $|1\rangle$ when measuring $|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle$?

> Amplitudes and probabilities are not the same thing.

1. [ ] $\beta$
1. [ ] $|\beta|$
1. [ ] $\beta^2$
1. [x] $|\beta|^2$
    > Correct: the Born rule gives $\Pr[|1\rangle] = |\beta|^2$. Amplitudes can be complex or negative, so we take the modulus squared.


### Which of these properties fundamentally distinguish a qubit from a classical bit?

> Several properties are purely quantum and have no classical analogue.

- [x] A qubit cannot be copied (no-cloning theorem)
    > Correct: it is impossible to duplicate an arbitrary unknown quantum state.
- [ ] A qubit can take only the values 0 or 1
    > Incorrect: that is precisely what characterizes a classical bit, not a qubit.
- [x] Measuring a qubit irreversibly changes its state
    > Correct: measurement causes state collapse, unlike reading a classical bit.
- [x] A qubit can be in a superposition of $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$
    > Correct: this is the superposition principle, absent from classical physics.
- [ ] A qubit is always in a deterministic state before measurement


### What is the state space of a system of $n$ qubits?

> Adding a single qubit doubles the power of the system.

1. [ ] $\mathbb{C}^n$
1. [ ] $\mathbb{C}^{2n}$
1. [x] $\mathbb{C}^{2^n}$
    > Correct: the Hilbert space of a system of $n$ qubits has dimension $2^n$. For $n = 64$, that is about $16 \times 10^{18}$ dimensions.
1. [ ] $\mathbb{R}^{2^n}$

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 2 — Composite quantum systems

### What is the dimension of the Hilbert space of two qubits?

> The space of two qubits is the tensor product of their individual spaces.

1. [ ] 2
1. [ ] 3
1. [x] 4
    > Correct: $\mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2$ has dimension $2 \times 2 = 4$, with basis $\{|00\rangle, |01\rangle, |10\rangle, |11\rangle\}$.
1. [ ] 8


### Put the elements of the natural two-qubit basis in standard lexicographic order.

> Think of increasing binary order.

1. $|00\rangle$
2. $|01\rangle$
3. $|10\rangle$
4. $|11\rangle$


### A two-qubit state is called a "product state" if and only if:

> Think about what independence between subsystems means.

1. [ ] All its amplitudes are real
1. [x] It can be written as $|\psi_1\rangle \otimes |\psi_2\rangle$ for some individual states $|\psi_1\rangle$ and $|\psi_2\rangle$
    > Correct: a product state describes two independent subsystems, each describable separately.
1. [ ] The sum of its amplitudes is zero
1. [ ] It satisfies $\alpha_{00} = \alpha_{11}$


### Which algebraic property does the tensor product satisfy?

> This property lets you chain tensor products unambiguously.

1. [ ] Commutative: $A \otimes B = B \otimes A$
1. [x] Associative: $A \otimes (B \otimes C) = (A \otimes B) \otimes C$
    > Correct: the tensor product is associative, which lets the description extend naturally to $n$ qubits.
1. [ ] Distributive over subtraction only
1. [ ] Invertible: $(A \otimes B)^{-1} = A^{-1} \otimes B^{-1}$ always

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 3 — Quantum entanglement

### What is the emblematic entangled state (Bell pair)?

> This state cannot be written as a tensor product of two individual states.

1. [ ] $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |01\rangle)$
1. [x] $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)$
    > Correct: this is the EPR pair (or Bell pair). If you try to factor it, you get a contradiction: $\alpha\beta' = 0$ and $\beta\alpha' = 0$ but $\alpha\alpha' = \beta\beta' = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \neq 0$.
1. [ ] $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle + |10\rangle)$
1. [ ] $|00\rangle$


### A state $\alpha_{00}|00\rangle + \alpha_{01}|01\rangle + \alpha_{10}|10\rangle + \alpha_{11}|11\rangle$ is a product state if and only if:

> This is a rank-1 condition on the coefficient matrix.

1. [ ] $\alpha_{00} = \alpha_{11}$
1. [ ] $\alpha_{00} + \alpha_{11} = \alpha_{01} + \alpha_{10}$
1. [x] $\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11} = \alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}$
    > Correct: this is the rank-1 condition. If it is satisfied, the state is a product state; otherwise, it is entangled.
1. [ ] $|\alpha_{00}|^2 = |\alpha_{11}|^2$


### Entanglement allows information to be transmitted faster than light.

> Think about what Bob can observe locally without classical communication.

1. [ ] True
1. [x] False
    > False: even though Bob’s qubit collapses instantaneously, each individual measurement outcome remains random. Bob cannot distinguish the statistics unless he receives Alice’s result through a classical channel.


### Which circuit generates a Bell pair from $|00\rangle$?

> Two gates suffice: one creates superposition, the other creates correlation.

1. [ ] CNOT then Hadamard
1. [x] Hadamard on qubit 1, then CNOT (qubit 1 control, qubit 2 target)
    > Correct: $|00\rangle \xrightarrow{H \otimes I} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle+|10\rangle) \xrightarrow{\text{CNOT}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)$.
1. [ ] CNOT then CNOT
1. [ ] Hadamard on both qubits simultaneously

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 4 — Quantum decoherence

### What is quantum decoherence?

> This phenomenon explains why macroscopic objects do not seem to be in superposition.

1. [ ] The energy loss of a qubit during a gate operation
1. [x] The loss of superposition and entanglement of a quantum system through interaction with its environment
    > Correct: the environment performs “involuntary measurements” on the system, gradually destroying quantum superpositions.
1. [ ] The error introduced by an imperfect unitary gate
1. [ ] The process of deliberately measuring a qubit


### Which of these consequences result directly from decoherence?

> Decoherence affects quantum computing capabilities at several levels.

- [x] Limitation of the maximum executable depth of quantum circuits
    > Correct: if the computation lasts longer than the coherence time, results are corrupted.
- [ ] Increased speed of quantum gates
- [x] Destruction of superpositions, leading to a loss of interference capability
    > Correct: without superposition, algorithmic advantage disappears.
- [x] Main source of errors in current quantum devices
    > Correct: decoherence is the main obstacle to building high-performance quantum computers.
- [ ] Impossibility of preparing the state $|0\rangle$


### Why do superconducting qubits operate at a few millikelvins?

> Think about the main source of disruptive interaction with the environment.

1. [ ] To increase the speed of quantum operations
1. [x] To minimize thermal interactions that cause decoherence
    > Correct: at very low temperature, thermal fluctuations are negligible, which increases qubit coherence times.
1. [ ] To reduce the physical size of qubits
1. [ ] To make state measurement easier


### What does the acronym NISQ mean?

> This term refers to the current era of quantum computing.

1. [ ] Non-Integrated Scalable Quantum
1. [x] Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum
    > Correct: NISQ refers to current quantum devices with around 100 controllable qubits but significant error rates, in particular due to decoherence.
1. [ ] New Integrated Superposition Qubit
1. [ ] Normalized Iterative Scalable Quantum

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
section: Question 5 — Effect of observing a qubit
text:
Question 5 — Effect of observing a qubit

### A qubit is prepared in the state $|+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle + |1\rangle)$. Apply an $H$ gate, then measure. What is the result?

> Remember that $H^2 = I$.

1. [ ] $|0\rangle$ or $|1\rangle$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each
1. [x] $|0\rangle$ with probability 1
    > Correct: $H|+\rangle = |0\rangle$. The $H$ gate is its own inverse, so $H(H|0\rangle) = |0\rangle$ and thus $H|+\rangle = |0\rangle$.
1. [ ] $|1\rangle$ with probability 1
1. [ ] $|+\rangle$ unchanged


### A circuit applies $H$, then an intermediate measurement, then $H$ again on a qubit initially in $|0\rangle$. What is the outcome of the final measurement?

> Compare with the case without an intermediate measurement. Does the measurement matter?

1. [x] $|0\rangle$ or $|1\rangle$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each
    > Correct: the intermediate measurement destroys the superposition and forces the qubit into $|0\rangle$ or $|1\rangle$. The second $H$ then creates a new superposition, giving a random result — unlike the case without intermediate measurement.
1. [ ] $|0\rangle$ with probability 1
1. [ ] $|1\rangle$ with probability 1
1. [ ] The state remains $|+\rangle$ after the second $H$


### Why does an intermediate measurement in a quantum circuit destroy interference?

> Think about what measurement does to the qubit’s superposition.

1. [ ] Because it consumes energy
1. [ ] Because it violates the circuit’s unitarity
1. [x] Because it forces the qubit into a classical state, eliminating the complex amplitudes that allow destructive cancellation of bad paths
    > Correct: interference relies on complex amplitudes that can cancel. Measurement collapses the state and removes that amplitude structure.
1. [ ] Because it flips all amplitudes


### To perfectly distinguish $|+\rangle$ from $|-\rangle$, what strategy should be used?

> A direct measurement in the $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ basis cannot differentiate them.

1. [ ] Measure directly in the computational basis $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$
1. [x] Apply $H$ then measure in the computational basis
    > Correct: $H|+\rangle = |0\rangle$ and $H|-\rangle = |1\rangle$, enabling perfect discrimination. A direct measurement would yield $|0\rangle$ or $|1\rangle$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ in both cases.
1. [ ] Apply $Z$ then measure
1. [ ] Apply $X$ then measure

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
section: Question 6 — Single- and two-qubit quantum gates
text:
Question 6 — Single- and two-qubit quantum gates

### Which of these properties is shared by all quantum gates?

> This property guarantees the physical consistency of quantum operations.

1. [ ] They are irreversible
1. [ ] They all have a classical analogue
1. [x] They are represented by unitary matrices ($UU^\dagger = I$)
    > Correct: unitarity guarantees norm preservation of quantum states and reversibility of operations.
1. [ ] They act only on a single qubit


### Which quantum gate plays the role of the classical NOT?

> It simply swaps the amplitudes of $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$.

1. [ ] Hadamard ($H$)
1. [ ] Pauli-$Z$
1. [x] Pauli-$X$
    > Correct: $X|0\rangle = |1\rangle$ and $X|1\rangle = |0\rangle$, exactly like a classical NOT on basis states.
1. [ ] Phase $S$


### Which of these statements about the Hadamard gate are correct?

> The $H$ gate has several remarkable properties related to superposition and measurement.

- [x] $H^2 = I$: applying $H$ twice is equivalent to doing nothing
    > Correct: $H$ is its own inverse ($H = H^\dagger$).
- [ ] $H$ is equivalent to the classical NOT gate
    > Incorrect: $H$ creates superpositions, which NOT does not. $X$ is the analogue of NOT.
- [x] $H|0\rangle = |+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle + |1\rangle)$
    > Correct: $H$ maps $|0\rangle$ to a perfect superposition.
- [x] $H$ has no classical analogue
    > Correct: creating superposition is a purely quantum phenomenon.
- [ ] $H$ cannot be combined with CNOT to create entanglement


### Applying CNOT to the state $|10\rangle$ produces which state?

> The first qubit is the control, the second is the target. Rule: if control = $|1\rangle$, flip the target.

1. [ ] $|10\rangle$
1. [x] $|11\rangle$
    > Correct: the control qubit is $|1\rangle$, so the target $|0\rangle$ flips to $|1\rangle$, giving $|11\rangle$.
1. [ ] $|00\rangle$
1. [ ] $|01\rangle$


### Which gate set is recognized as universal for quantum computing?

> A universal set can approximate any arbitrary unitary transformation.

1. [ ] $\{X, Y, Z\}$
1. [ ] $\{H, \text{CNOT}\}$
1. [x] $\{H, T, \text{CNOT}\}$
    > Correct: this set is universal. The $T$ gate is needed to reach arbitrary rotations on the Bloch sphere.
1. [ ] $\{\text{CNOT}\}$ alone is sufficient

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 7 — Quantum circuits

### Put in order the steps for executing a quantum circuit on a real quantum computer.

> Think about the flow from the program to the result.

1. The classical computer prepares and submits the circuit
2. The controller translates gates into physical pulses
3. The quantum register executes the operations
4. Measurement results are sent back to the classical computer


### Which fundamental structural property distinguishes a quantum circuit from a classical circuit?

> Think about what is preserved throughout a quantum circuit.

- [x] Fixed width: the same number of wires (qubits) runs through the entire circuit
    > Correct: reversibility of quantum operations forbids erasure, so you cannot “lose” a wire.
- [ ] Gates can take a variable number of inputs
- [x] The state space has dimension $2^n$ for $n$ qubits, versus $n$ classically
    > Correct: this is the main source of quantum computational power.
- [ ] Quantum circuits allow copying qubits between wires
- [x] All operations are reversible (except measurement)
    > Correct: quantum gates are unitary matrices, hence invertible. Only measurement is irreversible.


### A quantum circuit on $n$ qubits requires at least which of these elements to function correctly?

> Several conditions are necessary simultaneously.

- [x] Coherence times long enough to finish the computation
    > Correct: if the computation lasts longer than the coherence time, results are corrupted.
- [x] The ability to create entanglement between qubits
    > Correct: without entanglement (CNOT or equivalent), many quantum algorithms cannot be implemented.
- [ ] More than 1000 qubits for any useful computation
- [x] A physically available universal set of quantum gates
    > Correct: without a universal set, you cannot approximate all needed unitary transformations.

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 8 — Quantum algorithms

### What central mechanism allows quantum algorithms to be more efficient than their classical counterparts?

> This mechanism amplifies correct answers and cancels wrong ones before the final measurement.

1. [ ] Massive parallelism: the circuit tests all solutions simultaneously
1. [x] Quantum interference: amplitudes of correct answers add constructively, amplitudes of wrong answers cancel destructively
    > Correct: interference is the central mechanism. Superposition alone is not enough — without interference, measuring a superposition would just give a random outcome.
1. [ ] Teleporting data between qubits
1. [ ] Controlled decoherence


### Shor’s algorithm factors an $n$-bit integer with what complexity?

> Compare with the best known classical complexity, which is sub-exponential.

1. [ ] $O(2^n)$
1. [ ] $O(n^2)$
1. [x] $O(n^3 \log n)$ (polynomial)
    > Correct: Shor solves in polynomial time what requires sub-exponential time $O(e^{n^{1/3}})$ classically. This difference is spectacular: $10^{10}$ steps vs $10^{24}$ for a 30-digit number.
1. [ ] $O(\sqrt{n})$


### What speedup does Grover’s algorithm provide for unstructured search?

> This speedup is provably optimal for this type of problem.

1. [ ] Exponential: $O(\log N)$ instead of $O(N)$
1. [x] Quadratic: $O(\sqrt{N})$ instead of $O(N)$
    > Correct: Grover offers a quadratic speedup, provably optimal for unstructured search. That means no quantum algorithm can do better for this problem.
1. [ ] Logarithmic: $O(N \log N)$ instead of $O(N^2)$
1. [ ] Polynomial: $O(N^{1/3})$ instead of $O(N)$


### Why is quantum simulation considered the most promising application of quantum computers?

> Think about the classical cost of simulating a system of $N$ quantum particles.

1. [ ] Because it is the only proven practical application
1. [ ] Because it does not require error correction
1. [x] Because a quantum system of $N$ qubits can naturally simulate $N$ quantum particles, whereas a classical computer requires $2^N$ bits
    > Correct: this is Feynman’s dream (1981). For $N = 50$, that is $10^{15}$ classical equations — impossible in practice, but natural on a quantum device.
1. [ ] Because quantum simulators do not need calibration


### Can quantum computers efficiently solve all NP-hard problems?

> Think about which kinds of problems have proven quantum advantage.

1. [ ] Yes, thanks to Grover’s algorithm applied to solution search
1. [x] No, they excel on problems with exploitable mathematical structure (periodicity, uniform amplitude) but probably do not solve general NP-hard problems in polynomial time
    > Correct: quantum advantage has been proved for structured problems (factorization, search, simulation). For general NP-hard problems, no exponential advantage is known.
1. [ ] Yes, the exponential Hilbert space allows exploring all solutions simultaneously
1. [ ] No, because Shor’s algorithm works only for factorization

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 9 — Quantum volume

### Why is the raw number of qubits insufficient to compare two quantum computers?

> A device with many noisy qubits can be less useful than a smaller but higher-quality device.

1. [ ] Because all qubits must be of the same physical type to be comparable
1. [ ] Because only execution time matters
1. [x] Because a device with many qubits but a high error rate can perform worse than a device with fewer, higher-quality qubits
    > Correct: that is precisely the motivation for quantum volume, which captures the tension between quantity and quality.
1. [ ] Because superconducting qubits and trapped ions cannot be compared


### What does the quantum volume $\tilde{V}_Q = \min[N, d(N)]^2$ measure?

> This formula captures the tension between two limiting factors.

1. [ ] The maximum number of qubits available on the processor
1. [ ] The average execution speed of quantum gates
1. [x] The size of the largest square circuit (number of qubits × depth) executable reliably
    > Correct: quantum volume is limited by the weaker factor between width (number of qubits) and achievable depth. A computer with many qubits but little depth is penalized.
1. [ ] The average gate error rate


### In June 2020, Honeywell reached a quantum volume of 64 with only 6 qubits, while IBM needed 27 for the same score. What main conclusion can be drawn?

> This result illustrates the central message of quantum volume.

1. [ ] Honeywell has a physically superior technology to IBM
1. [x] Qubit quality (low error rate, large achievable depth) can compensate for the number of qubits
    > Correct: this is the essence of quantum volume. Six very high-quality qubits can be more useful than 27 noisy qubits.
1. [ ] Quantum volume favors small systems
1. [ ] IBM had more qubits but an architecture unfavorable to this metric

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 10 — Helstrom–Holevo bound

### What is the maximum probability of discriminating two identical quantum states ($|\psi_a\rangle = |\psi_b\rangle$) according to the Helstrom–Holevo bound?

> If the two states are identical, no measurement can distinguish them.

1. [ ] $1$ (perfect discrimination always possible)
1. [x] $\frac{1}{2}$ (no better than guessing)
    > Correct: $\theta = 0$, so $\sin\theta = 0$ and $p = \frac{1}{2}(1 + 0) = \frac{1}{2}$. Discriminating identical states is impossible.
1. [ ] $0$ (always wrong)
1. [ ] $\frac{3}{4}$


### According to the Helstrom–Holevo bound, what is the maximum probability of discriminating $|0\rangle$ and $|+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle + |1\rangle)$?

> First compute the inner product $\langle 0|+\rangle$, then the angle $\theta$.

1. [ ] $\frac{1}{2}$
1. [ ] $\frac{3}{4}$
1. [x] $\frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \approx 85\%$
    > Correct: $\langle 0|+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, i.e. $\theta = 45°$. The bound gives $\frac{1}{2}(1 + \sin 45°) \approx 85\%$. The naive strategy (computational basis) gives only 75%.
1. [ ] $1$ (perfect discrimination because the states are different)


### Is the Helstrom–Holevo bound only an upper bound, or is it achieved by a concrete measurement?

> Think about the difference between a bound and an exact optimal value.

1. [ ] It is an upper bound that is not achieved in general
1. [x] The bound is exactly achieved: there exists a measurement (in the eigenbasis of $|\psi_a\rangle\langle\psi_a| - |\psi_b\rangle\langle\psi_b|$) that achieves it
    > Correct: the Helstrom–Holevo bound is the exact optimal value, not merely an upper bound. The optimal measurement uses eigenvectors of the difference operator.
1. [ ] The bound is reached only if the states are orthogonal
1. [ ] The bound is never reached for non-orthogonal states

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 11 — Quantum no-signalling principle

### Alice and Bob share a Bell pair. Alice measures her qubit (outcome unknown to Bob). What is the distribution of Bob’s measurements on his qubit?

> Bob has no way to know what Alice did.

1. [ ] $p_B(0) = 1$ if Alice obtained $|0\rangle$, $p_B(0) = 0$ if Alice obtained $|1\rangle$
1. [x] $p_B(0) = p_B(1) = \frac{1}{2}$, identical to the case where Alice does not measure
    > Correct: from Bob’s perspective (he does not know Alice’s outcome), his qubit is in a statistical mixture $\frac{1}{2}|0\rangle + \frac{1}{2}|1\rangle$. His statistics are indistinguishable from the case where Alice does not measure.
1. [ ] $p_B(0) = \frac{3}{4}$
1. [ ] The distribution depends on Alice’s measurement basis


### Why doesn’t Bob’s instantaneous collapse (when Alice measures) enable superluminal communication?

> No-signalling is consistent with special relativity.

1. [ ] Because collapse is not really instantaneous
1. [x] Because Bob cannot detect the collapse without knowing Alice’s outcome, which can reach him only through a classical channel limited by $c$
    > Correct: collapse is real but locally undetectable. Bob observes uniform statistics in all cases. Only classical communication of Alice’s outcome would let him exploit the correlation.
1. [ ] Because the Bell pair produces only classical correlations
1. [ ] Because quantum mechanics forbids correlations at a distance


### What link exists between the no-cloning principle and the no-signalling principle?

> If one were violated, the other would be too.

1. [ ] They are independent and have no logical relation
1. [x] They are mutually consistent: if one could clone a qubit, one could use state tomography to detect collapse and transmit information superluminally
    > Correct: with cloning, Bob could make many copies of his qubit and perform tomography to detect a state change, violating no-signalling. The two principles form a coherent set.
1. [ ] No-cloning implies no-signalling, but not conversely
1. [ ] No-signalling follows only from Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 12 — Quantum no-cloning principle

### What is the statement of the no-cloning theorem?

> This result applies only to unknown, arbitrary states.

1. [ ] It is impossible to measure the same qubit twice
1. [ ] It is impossible to copy a qubit into another qubit in the same circuit
1. [x] There is no unitary transformation $U$ such that $U(|\psi\rangle|0\rangle) = |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle$ for all states $|\psi\rangle$
    > Correct: no-cloning forbids copying an arbitrary unknown quantum state. Orthogonal or identical states can technically be “copied”, but that corresponds to classical information.
1. [ ] It is impossible to prepare two qubits in the same state


### In the proof of the no-cloning theorem, which equation leads to the contradiction?

> The proof uses only linearity and the isometry of $U$.

1. [ ] $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = 0$ for all $|\phi\rangle$
1. [ ] $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = 2(\langle\psi|\phi\rangle)^2$
1. [x] $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = (\langle\psi|\phi\rangle)^2$
    > Correct: this equation $x = x^2$ has only two solutions ($x = 0$ or $x = 1$), ruling out any pair of distinct non-orthogonal states. That is the contradiction.
1. [ ] $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = \sqrt{\langle\psi|\phi\rangle}$


### Which of these statements about consequences of no-cloning are correct?

> No-cloning impacts both cryptography and error correction.

- [x] The security of BB84 relies on the fact that an eavesdropper cannot silently copy the intercepted qubits
    > Correct: no-cloning is the cornerstone of QKD security.
- [ ] Quantum error correction is impossible because of no-cloning
    > Incorrect: QEC is possible, but it uses entanglement instead of direct copying.
- [x] Quantum error correction cannot use the classical strategy of simple repetition
    > Correct: you cannot create three copies of $|\psi\rangle$ to do majority voting. Entangled codes are needed.
- [x] Cloning would enable super-compression of information, violating Holevo’s theorem
    > Correct: with cloning, one could encode and decode arbitrarily more than 1 bit per qubit, which Holevo forbids.

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 13 — Quantum no-deleting principle

### The no-deleting principle is the time-reversal dual of no-cloning. What does that mean concretely?

> Think about the time directions of the two forbidden transformations.

1. [ ] The two principles are equivalent and state the same prohibition
1. [ ] No-cloning concerns logical qubits, no-deleting concerns physical qubits
1. [x] No-cloning forbids $|\psi\rangle|0\rangle \to |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle$ (1→2 copies) and no-deleting forbids $|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle \to |\psi\rangle|0\rangle$ (2→1 copies)
    > Correct: the two transformations are inverses of each other. Unitary reversibility ensures that forbidding one implies forbidding the other.
1. [ ] The two principles are independent and can be violated separately


### How does the reversibility of quantum mechanics justify no-deleting from no-cloning?

> Reversibility is a fundamental property of unitary transformations.

1. [ ] Reversibility forbids all transformations that change the number of qubits
1. [x] If $\tilde{U}$ could delete (2→1 copies), its adjoint $\tilde{U}^\dagger$ could clone (1→2 copies), which is forbidden by no-cloning
    > Correct: $\tilde{U}^\dagger$ is a valid unitary transformation. If $\tilde{U}$ existed, $\tilde{U}^\dagger$ would violate no-cloning, a contradiction.
1. [ ] Reversibility has no logical link to no-deleting
1. [ ] Reversibility forbids only measurements, not deletions


### What is a practical implication of no-deleting for designing quantum circuits?

> Think about ancilla (auxiliary) qubits used in quantum algorithms.

1. [ ] You can simply ignore ancilla qubits after use
1. [ ] Ancilla qubits must be measured at the end of every gate
1. [x] Ancilla qubits cannot be “erased”; they must be reset by inverse operations ($U^\dagger$) before being reused
    > Correct: no-deleting forbids unitary erasure. Ancilla qubits must be returned to their initial state via inverse operations, which complicates algorithm design.
1. [ ] Ancilla qubits can be teleported out of the circuit to be destroyed

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 14 — Applications of quantum computing

### What is the central mechanism of Shor’s algorithm for factoring $N$?

> Factoring is reduced to another problem that is easier quantumly.

1. [ ] Quantum exhaustive search over all divisors of $N$
1. [ ] Simulation of the “decay” of a number into its factors
1. [x] Reduce factoring to finding the period of $f(s) = x^s \bmod N$, solved efficiently by the QFT
    > Correct: once the period $l$ is found, simple classical computations (GCD) yield the factors. The QFT concentrates amplitude on multiples of $2^n/l$ in polynomial time.
1. [ ] Apply Grover directly to candidate divisors


### Why is Shor’s algorithm a threat to RSA cryptography?

> RSA rests on a number-theory problem.

1. [ ] Because Shor can solve any NP-hard problem
1. [x] Because RSA security relies on the assumed hardness of factoring large integers, which Shor solves in polynomial time
    > Correct: to break RSA-2048, about 8000 logical qubits with error correction would be required. This capability could exist within the next 5 to 10 years.
1. [ ] Because Shor directly decrypts RSA messages
1. [ ] Because Shor breaks all symmetric encryption systems


### For which of these applications is a quantum advantage not yet rigorously proven?

> Some applications are promising but their advantage remains to be formally demonstrated.

1. [ ] Integer factorization (Shor)
1. [ ] Unstructured search (Grover)
1. [ ] Simulation of quantum systems
1. [x] General combinatorial optimization (QAOA and variants)
    > Correct: although quantum optimization is sometimes presented as a “killer application”, a quantum advantage over the best classical algorithms for general optimization problems has not yet been proven.

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 15 — Quantum teleportation

### What resources are required to quantum-teleport a qubit?

> Teleportation combines quantum and classical resources.

- [x] A Bell pair (one half for Alice, the other for Bob)
    > Correct: the Bell pair is the essential quantum resource.
- [ ] A direct quantum channel between Alice and Bob
    > Incorrect: teleportation uses a classical channel, not a quantum channel, for the final transmission.
- [x] A classical channel to send 2 bits
    > Correct: without the 2 classical bits, Bob cannot correct his qubit.
- [ ] Knowledge of the amplitudes $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of the state to be teleported
    > Incorrect: Alice does not know $\alpha$ and $\beta$; that is precisely why she cannot send them classically.
- [x] The message qubit $|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle$ that Alice wants to transmit
    > Correct: this is the state to be teleported.


### Put in order the steps of the quantum teleportation protocol.

> Alice acts first, then communicates, then Bob corrects.

1. Alice applies CNOT (message qubit → her qubit of the pair)
2. Alice applies $H$ on the message qubit
3. Alice measures her two qubits and obtains 2 classical bits
4. Alice sends the 2 bits to Bob via the classical channel
5. Bob applies the corrections ($X$ if $b_0=1$, $Z$ if $b_1=1$)


### After teleportation, does Alice still have the state $|\psi\rangle$?

> Think about the no-cloning theorem and what measurement does to Alice’s state.

1. [ ] Yes, Alice and Bob both have $|\psi\rangle$
1. [x] No, Alice’s state is irreversibly destroyed when she measures
    > Correct: upon measurement, Alice’s message qubit collapses. No-cloning is respected: at no time do two copies of $|\psi\rangle$ coexist.
1. [ ] Yes, if Alice obtained outcome 00
1. [ ] No, but Alice can reconstruct it from the 2 bits sent to Bob


### Does quantum teleportation allow faster-than-light communication?

> Examine what would be necessary for Bob to use his qubit.

1. [ ] Yes, Bob’s qubit collapses instantaneously regardless of distance
1. [x] No, because Bob needs Alice’s 2 classical bits to correct his qubit, and those bits can travel at most at the speed of light
    > Correct: without the classical bits, Bob’s qubit is in a statistical mixture with no usable information about $|\psi\rangle$. Teleportation is limited by the speed of the classical channel.
1. [ ] Yes, if the distance between Alice and Bob is less than 1 km
1. [ ] No, because teleportation destroys the state before it can be transmitted

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 16 — Superdense coding

### In superdense coding, how many classical bits can Alice transmit to Bob by sending a single qubit?

> The result may seem paradoxical in light of Holevo’s theorem.

1. [ ] 1 bit (same as a qubit without entanglement)
1. [x] 2 bits
    > Correct: thanks to the shared Bell pair, Alice encodes 2 bits into which Bell state the pair occupies, which Bob can decode by measuring both qubits jointly.
1. [ ] 3 bits
1. [ ] An arbitrary number of bits


### What operation does Alice apply to send the message "11" in superdense coding?

> Alice must transform $|\Phi^+\rangle$ into $|\Psi^-\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|10\rangle - |01\rangle)$.

1. [ ] Identity $I$
1. [ ] Gate $X$ only
1. [ ] Gate $Z$ only
1. [x] Gate $XZ$ (apply $Z$ then $X$, or their product)
    > Correct: applying $XZ$ on the first qubit of $|\Phi^+\rangle$ yields $|\Psi^-\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|10\rangle - |01\rangle)$, which corresponds to message "11".


### Why is entanglement indispensable for superdense coding?

> Without entanglement, Holevo’s theorem applies directly.

1. [ ] Because it speeds up transmitting the qubit through the quantum channel
1. [x] Because without a shared Bell pair, a qubit can carry only 1 classical bit (Holevo’s theorem). The information is encoded in the global, non-local Bell state.
    > Correct: the sent qubit alone does not contain the 2 bits. It is the set {sent qubit, Bob’s qubit} that contains them, thanks to non-local correlation.
1. [ ] Because it reduces noise on the quantum channel
1. [ ] Because Bob cannot measure his qubit without entanglement


### How does Bob decode the message in superdense coding?

> He must “disentangle” the pair to recover a computational basis state.

1. [ ] He measures his qubit directly in the computational basis
1. [ ] He applies $H$ to his qubit, then measures
1. [x] He applies CNOT (Alice’s qubit as control) then $H$ on Alice’s qubit, then measures in the computational basis
    > Correct: this circuit implements the inverse Bell transform, mapping each of the 4 Bell states to one of the 4 basis states $\{|00\rangle, |01\rangle, |10\rangle, |11\rangle\}$.
1. [ ] He waits for Alice to communicate the result over a classical channel

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 17 — Quantum key distribution (QKD / BB84)

### Which security property distinguishes a one-time pad encrypted with a QKD key from RSA?

> Think about the underlying assumptions of each system.

1. [ ] The one-time pad is faster to implement
1. [ ] RSA relies on mathematical operations that the one-time pad does not use
1. [x] A one-time pad provides information-theoretic security (mathematically proven), independent of the adversary’s computing power, whereas RSA provides only computational security
    > Correct: RSA security would collapse if factoring became easy (Shor’s algorithm). A one-time pad with a QKD key is provably secure regardless of adversary power.
1. [ ] RSA is vulnerable to classical attacks, not quantum attacks


### In BB84, why do Alice and Bob discard about half of the bits after the exchange?

> This corresponds to the “sifting” step.

1. [ ] To correct errors introduced by channel noise
1. [x] Because they keep only the bits for which they used the same basis, which happens on average half the time
    > Correct: Alice randomly chooses an encoding basis; Bob randomly chooses a measurement basis. When bases differ, Bob’s outcome is random and unusable.
1. [ ] To increase the length of the final key
1. [ ] By convention to simplify the protocol


### An eavesdropper Eve intercepts BB84 qubits, measures them in a random basis, and resends new qubits to Bob. What error rate does she introduce on Alice and Bob’s shared raw key?

> Eve has a 50% chance to choose the wrong basis, and then she disturbs the qubit 50% of the time.

1. [ ] 0% (no disturbance if Eve resends correctly)
1. [ ] 10%
1. [x] 25%
    > Correct: Eve chooses the wrong basis in 50% of cases. When she is wrong, she introduces an error on the kept bits (where Alice and Bob used matching bases) in 50% of those cases. So $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = 25\%$ errors on the raw key.
1. [ ] 50%


### Why is the no-cloning theorem crucial for BB84 security?

> Think about the attack Eve would try if cloning were possible.

1. [ ] It prevents Bob from making multiple measurements on the same qubit
1. [x] It prevents Eve from keeping a copy of the qubit and measuring it only after the bases are publicly announced, which would let her obtain the information without disturbing Bob’s qubit
    > Correct: without no-cloning, Eve could store a perfect copy and wait until the basis is publicly announced to measure in the correct basis, leaving no trace.
1. [ ] It forbids Alice from preparing the same state multiple times
1. [ ] It guarantees that the quantum channel is noiseless

title: Quantum Computing — Review quiz
text:
Question 18 — Quantum error correction

### Which of these obstacles make quantum error correction harder than classical error correction?

> Three fundamental obstacles must be overcome simultaneously.

- [x] No-cloning forbids simply replicating the state for majority voting
    > Correct: you cannot directly create three copies of $|\psi\rangle$. Entanglement replaces copying.
- [x] Direct measurement to detect errors would destroy the protected superposition
    > Correct: parity measurements are designed to reveal the error without revealing the amplitudes $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
- [x] Quantum errors are continuous (arbitrary perturbation of $\alpha, \beta$), whereas classical errors are only discrete
    > Correct: error digitization by parity measurements solves this by projecting the continuous error onto a discrete case.
- [ ] It is impossible to detect errors without measuring each qubit directly
- [ ] Quantum circuits cannot correct more than one error per 1000 gates


### In the 3-qubit quantum repetition code, how is the state $|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle$ encoded?

> Careful: this is not three copies of $|\psi\rangle$.

1. [ ] $(\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle)^{\otimes 3} = \alpha^3|000\rangle + \ldots + \beta^3|111\rangle$
1. [x] $\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle$
    > Correct: this entangled state is fundamentally different from three copies. No-cloning is not violated because we did not create $|\psi\rangle \otimes |\psi\rangle \otimes |\psi\rangle$.
1. [ ] $\alpha|001\rangle + \beta|110\rangle$
1. [ ] $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(|000\rangle + |001\rangle + |010\rangle)$


### Why do parity measurements detect errors without destroying superposition?

> The question is: what information do they reveal exactly?

1. [ ] Because they are applied very quickly
1. [ ] Because they disturb only the ancilla qubits
1. [x] Because they reveal only whether two qubits are equal or different (the syndrome), without ever revealing the absolute values of amplitudes $\alpha$ and $\beta$
    > Correct: a parity measurement between qubits 1 and 2 yields 0 (same) or 1 (different), without indicating whether the qubits are $|0\rangle$ or $|1\rangle$. Information about $\alpha$ and $\beta$ remains intact.
1. [ ] Because they project onto the Bell basis rather than the computational basis


### The 9-qubit Shor code can correct an arbitrary continuous error on a single qubit. What mechanism makes this possible?

> This mechanism turns a continuous problem into a discrete one.

1. [ ] Redundancy over 9 qubits makes errors unlikely
1. [ ] The Shor code detects only $X$ errors and ignores $Z$
1. [x] Error digitization: parity measurements project any continuous error onto one of 4 discrete cases ($I$, $X$, $Z$, $XZ$), each correctable by a deterministic unitary operation
    > Correct: any error decomposes as $k \cdot I + l \cdot X + m \cdot Z + n \cdot XZ$. Parity measurements select one case and enable exact correction.
1. [ ] The Shor code repeats measurement until obtaining a consistent result


### What advantage does the Steane code have over the Shor code while maintaining the same correction guarantees?

> Compare the number of physical qubits needed per logical qubit.

1. [ ] The Steane code corrects more simultaneous errors
1. [x] The Steane code uses only 7 physical qubits per logical qubit (rate $1/7$) versus 9 for the Shor code (rate $1/9$), thanks to the CSS construction from the Hamming (7,4) code
    > Correct: the Steane code provides the same protection ($X$, $Z$, $XZ$, continuous errors) with better efficiency. Both reduce error rate from $p_e$ to $O(p_e^2)$.
1. [ ] The Steane code works without ancilla qubits
1. [ ] The Steane code does not need parity measurements

text:
Shor’s algorithm (Factorization)

Key idea
Reduce factorization to period search of a modular function:
\[f(s) = x^s \bmod N\]


Steps

Choose \(x\) co-first with \(N\)
Find the period \(l\) of \(f\) via QFT
Calculate \(\gcd(x^{l/2} \pm 1,\ N)\) → factors of \(N\)
Check ; otherwise start again



Basic theorem
If \(a \not\equiv \pm b \pmod{N}\) but \(a^2 \equiv b^2 \pmod{N}\) then \(\gcd(a+b, N)\) is a factor of \(N\)


Complexity



Method
Complexity




Classic (best)
\(O(\exp(n^{1/3}))\)


Shor (quantum)
\(O(n^3 \log n)\)





Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT)
\[U_{QFT} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{y=0}^{N-1}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1} \omega_N^{xy}|y\rangle\langle x|, \quad \omega_N = e^{2\pi i/N}\]

Extract the period by quantum interference
Core of Shor’s algorithm

title: Fundamental Properties of Quantum Computing — Quiz
text:
### What happens when we measure a qubit in the |1> state in the computational base?

> Remember the decomposition |1> = 0|0> + 1|1> and Born's rule.

1. [ ] We obtain 0 with probability 1
1. [ ] We obtain 0 or 1 with probability 1/2 each
1. [x] We obtain 1 with probability 1
    > Correct: |1> = 0|0> + 1|1>, so p(measure 1) = |1|^2 = 1. There is no quantity, it is classical information.
1. [ ] The result is indeterminable


### What is the necessary and sufficient condition to perfectly distinguish two quantum states by a measurement?

> Think about the geometric relationship between the two state vectors.

1. [ ] States must have the same standard
1. [ ] The states must be in the computational base
1. [x] States must be orthogonal
    > Correct: two states are perfectly distinguishable if and only if their scalar product is zero, that is to say if they are orthogonal.
1. [ ] States must have real amplitudes


### What does the Helstrom-Holevo Bound express?

> This bound relates the angle between two states to a maximum probability.

1. [ ] The maximum number of qubits measurable simultaneously
1. [x] The maximum probability of correctly distinguishing two non-orthogonal states
    > Correct: if || = cos(theta), then p_succes <= (1 + sin(theta)) / 2. This is the fundamental limit of state discrimination.
1. [ ] The minimum fidelity between two entangled states
1. [ ] The maximum speed of quantum information transmission


### What does the No-Cloning Theorem state?

> Think about what a unitary cloning operator should satisfy for any arbitrary state.

1. [ ] It is impossible to measure a quantum state without modifying it
1. [ ] It is impossible to transmit a quantum state by entanglement
1. [ ] It is impossible to copy a qubit in the |0> state
1. [x] It is impossible to copy an arbitrary quantum state by a unitary transformation
    > Correct: no unitary U can satisfy U(|psi>|0>) = |psi>|psi> for all |psi>. The proof follows from the linearity of quantum mechanics.


### What does the No-Signalling Principle say?

> Think of the scenario of Alice and Bob sharing a pair of Bells.

1. [ ] Entangled qubits cannot be physically separated
1. [ ] Measuring a qubit always destroys entanglement
1. [x] Quantum entanglement does not allow information to be transmitted faster than light
    > Correct: Even if Alice collapses Bob's state by her measurement, Bob's statistics remain the same. It cannot detect Alice's measurement without a classical signal.
1. [ ] Two entangled qubits can never have different states after measurement


### What is the temporal dual of the principle of non-cloning?

> The reversibility of quantum computing creates a symmetry between creation and destruction of copies.

1. [ ] The principle of non-signalling
1. [ ] Bell's theorem
1. [x] The No-Deleting Theorem
    > Correct: non-cloning prohibits going from 1 to 2 copies, non-deleting prohibits going from 2 to 1 copy. They are linked by unitary reversibility.
1. [ ] The Helstrom-Holevo terminal

1. [ ] It is impossible to measure a quantum state without modifying it
1. [ ] It is impossible to transmit a quantum state by entanglement
1. [ ] It is impossible to copy a qubit in the |0> state
1. [x] It is impossible to copy an arbitrary quantum state by a unitary transformation
    > Correct: no unitary U can satisfy U(|psi>|0>) = |psi>|psi> for all |psi>. The proof follows from the linearity of quantum mechanics.


### What does the No-Signalling Principle say?

> Think of the scenario of Alice and Bob sharing a pair of Bells.

1. [ ] Entangled qubits cannot be physically separated
1. [ ] Measuring a qubit always destroys entanglement
1. [x] Quantum entanglement does not allow information to be transmitted faster than light
    > Correct: Even if Alice collapses Bob's state by her measurement, Bob's statistics remain the same. It cannot detect Alice's measurement without a classical signal.
1. [ ] Two entangled qubits can never have different states after measurement


### What is the temporal dual of the principle of non-cloning?

> The reversibility of quantum computing creates a symmetry between creation and destruction of copies.

1. [ ] The principle of non-signalling
1. [ ] Bell's theorem
1. [x] The No-Deleting Theorem
    > Correct: non-cloning prohibits going from 1 to 2 copies, non-deleting prohibits going from 2 to 1 copy. They are linked by unitary reversibility.
1. [ ] The Helstrom-Holevo terminal

title: Fundamental Properties of Quantum Computing — Quiz

Level 2 — Comprehension

### Which of these statements are correct regarding the distinction of quantum states?

> Think about the two cases: orthogonal vs. non-orthogonal states, and what the bound guarantees.

- [x] Two orthogonal states can always be distinguished perfectly
    > Correct: Just apply U-dagger to align the states to the computational basis, then measure.
- [ ] Two non-orthogonal states can never be distinguished
    > Incorrect: partial information can be obtained. The Helstrom-Holevo bound gives the maximum probability of success, which is always strictly greater than 1/2.
- [x] The Helstrom-Holevo limit is always reached for an optimal measurement base
    > Correct: the bound is exact and reached by measuring in the basis of the eigenvectors of |psi_a> Incorrect: the optimal strategy depends on the states to be distinguished. The computational basis is rarely optimal for generic non-orthogonal states.


### When trying to distinguish between |0> and |+> by measuring in the computational base, which statement is true?

> Analyzes the probabilities of each outcome for each of the two states.

1. [ ] If we measure 0, we are certain that the state is |0>
1. [x] If we measure 1, we are certain that the state is |+>
    > Correct: |0> never gives the outcome 1. So if we measure 1, the state was necessarily |+>. On the other hand, outcome 0 does not allow us to conclude with certainty.
1. [ ] The probability of success is 85%
1. [ ] This strategy is optimal


### In the proof of the non-signaling principle for a Bell pair, why can't Bob know if Alice measured?

> Compare Bob's statistics in the two cases.

1. [ ] Because Bob is too far from Alice
1. [ ] Because Alice's measurement destroys the entanglement before Bob measures
1. [x] Because Bob's measurement probabilities are the same whether Alice measured or not
    > Correct: in both cases, Bob measures 0 or 1 with probability 1/2. In the absence of traditional communication, statistics are indistinguishable.
1. [ ] Because Bob does not have access to Alice's measurement base


### Why is quantum computing called reversible (Reversible Computing), except for measurement?

> Think about the nature of the transformations used between measurements.

1. [ ] Because qubits can spontaneously return to their initial state
1. [ ] Because we can always undo a quantum measurement
1. [x] Because the transformations between measurements are unitary, therefore invertible
    > Correct: every unitary U admits an inverse U-dagger. Measurement is the only irreversible operation in quantum computing.
1. [ ] Because quantum information is always preserved, even during measurements


### Which of these situations correctly illustrates the strategy of asymmetric discrimination (Unambiguous Discrimination)?

> In this strategy, we align a measurement vector with one of the states.

1. [ ] We measure in the base which maximizes the average probability of success
1. [ ] The measurement is repeated a large number of times to reduce the error
1. [x] We align a measurement base vector with one of the states, sometimes obtaining absolute certainty on the other
    > Correct: if |psi_a> is orthogonal to a vector of the measurement base, obtaining the corresponding outcome certifies that the state was |psi_b>. On the other hand, the overall probability of success is lower.
1. [ ] We use an ancillary qubit to improve discrimination


### Which of these consequences would result from a hypothetical cloning theorem?

> List what a universal clone operator would allow.

- [x] Violation of the principle of non-signalling
    > Correct: With cloning, Alice could send superluminal information, which would violate relativity and non-signaling.
- [x] The compression of an infinite amount of classical information into a single qubit
    > Correct: we could encode a long message in a qubit state, clone it infinitely, then reconstruct the message using quantum tomography.
- [ ] The possibility of perfectly distinguishing any quantum state
    > Incorrect: Even with cloning, the Helstrom-Holevo bound would still apply on each individual copy.
- [x] Quantum error correction would become trivial
    > Correct: if we could clone, classical redundancy would be sufficient to correct errors, as in classical calculation.
